fixes.explanation: That's it. Jonathan says, "Go in peace, for the two of us have sworn in the name of the LORD, saying, ‘May the LORD be a witness between you and me, and between your descendants and mine forever.’" (1 Samuel 20:42). He sends David off with peace and a promise. The oath goes with him.

Not quite, friend. David is asking the opposite. He says, "What have I done? What is my iniquity? How have I sinned against your father, that he wants to take my life?" (1 Samuel 20:1). A man who knew his crime wouldn't be asking for the list. I think David is confused and scared, and he runs to Jonathan, Saul's son, with his questions.

Yes, grieved. David says Saul has said, "Jonathan must not know of this, or he will be grieved." (1 Samuel 20:3). That's David's account of why Saul keeps Jonathan out of it. It's the secret Jonathan says he knows nothing about (1 Samuel 20:2).

Close to the neighborhood, but not the word, friend. David says Saul keeps it quiet "…or he will be grieved." (1 Samuel 20:3). Embarrassed is about how you look. Grieved is about how much it hurts, and that's what David says Saul expects Jonathan to feel.

True, and notice how bold David gets. He says, "If there is iniquity in me, then kill me yourself; why should you bring me to your father?" (1 Samuel 20:8). He'd rather face Jonathan, his covenant friend, than be handed over to Saul. I think that's a man who trusts his friend.
Nice loyal idea, but it's not what Jonathan swears. He says he'll "…tell you and send you on your way in safety." (1 Samuel 20:13). He promises to send David away, not to stand watch.

True. Jonathan asks David, "…do not ever cut off your loving devotion from my household—not even when the LORD cuts off every one of David’s enemies from the face of the earth." (1 Samuel 20:15). Jonathan is thinking about his family's future, even after David's enemies are gone. That's a friend planning ahead.
That's the reason the text gives. It says Jonathan "…had David reaffirm his vow out of love for him, for Jonathan loved David as he loved himself." (1 Samuel 20:17). Love is what the verse names.

Bethlehem is in the story, but only as the excuse Jonathan is to give the king (1 Samuel 20:6). Jonathan tells David to "…remain beside the stone Ezel." (1 Samuel 20:19). You can't meet a friend at an excuse, baker. Ezel is the spot.

Nice try, friend, but no tree gets a part here. Jonathan says, "…remain beside the stone Ezel." (1 Samuel 20:19). It's the place David hid when this trouble began. Gibeah doesn't even get a cameo in that verse.

Safe is right. Jonathan tells David that if he tells the boy the arrows are on this side of him, David should come, because "…it is safe for you, and there is no danger." (1 Samuel 20:21). Arrows closer means come out. I'd have needed a diagram, but David gets it.

Not quite, friend. Saul says, "For as long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established." (1 Samuel 20:31). The word is kingdom. I think Saul is worried about the crown.

Beyond is right. "…Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him." (1 Samuel 20:36). That's the signal he and David agreed on for "…you must go…" (1 Samuel 20:22). The boy did not know anything about the arrangement (1 Samuel 20:39).
